options: Arrange urgent ultrasound-guided hydrostatic reduction and add antibiotics only if the reduction proves unsuccessful.
Attempt pneumatic enema reduction with surgical backup, because this treatment is usually successful in infants.
Repeat specialist ultrasound before proceeding, as bowel location must be confirmed despite the radiographic findings.
Give analgesia and fluid resuscitation, then observe for discharge if the child's vital signs become normal.
Resuscitate, administer appropriate IV antibiotics and involve paediatric surgery immediately for operative management.
explanations: Enema reduction is reasonable in uncomplicated intussusception but is contraindicated in suspected perforation or peritonitis. The free air makes radiological reduction unsafe.
Although pneumatic reduction is successful in many stable cases, this infant is shocked and has radiographic perforation. Proceeding risks worsening contamination and delaying surgery.
A repeat scan may add anatomical detail but is not the priority when shock, peritonitis and free gas demand treatment. Additional imaging should not postpone urgent care.
Resuscitation and analgesia are necessary but insufficient. Improvement after a fluid bolus cannot make a perforated bowel safe for discharge or observation alone.

Correct: begin ABC resuscitation, IV access, fluids, analgesia, nil by mouth and suitable IV antibiotics. Contact paediatric surgery and anaesthesia urgently for operative assessment and likely laparotomy.
pearl: Air or contrast enema reduction is contraindicated by shock, peritonitis, bowel perforation or clinical instability.
pivot: In a stable child without peritoneal signs or free air, specialist-guided air enema is commonly preferred with surgical backup.

steps: Resuscitate
Assess ABCs, provide monitoring and correct hypoperfusion using paediatric protocol-based isotonic boluses.
Protect
Keep nil by mouth, provide analgesia, consider nasogastric decompression and obtain relevant preoperative tests.
Escalate
Give appropriate IV antibiotics and summon paediatric surgery and anaesthesia urgently.
Operate
Proceed to specialist-directed surgical management rather than contrast or air enema reduction.
management.safety: Do not attempt reduction by enema if perforation, peritonitis or shock is present.
management.local: Follow the linked Australian guidance and current local specialist protocols.

stem: A 33-week G1P0 has a 70-second generalised tonic-clonic seizure on the antenatal ward. After the convulsion, she is drowsy with BP 172/116 mmHg and brisk reflexes. No known epilepsy or previous magnesium treatment is documented. The fetal heart rate transiently slows immediately after the seizure.
ask: Which combined response is MOST appropriate after immediate ABC assessment?
options: Give magnesium sulfate, control severe blood pressure and coordinate timely birth after maternal stabilisation.
Start phenytoin maintenance and delay blood-pressure treatment until brain imaging excludes intracranial pathology.
Perform an immediate caesarean before treating recurrent seizure risk or the severe blood-pressure elevation.
Lower blood pressure using appropriate medication and give magnesium only if another convulsion occurs.
Use diazepam as routine seizure prophylaxis and continue antenatal observation without a birth plan.
explanations: Correct: treat eclampsia with magnesium sulfate and an appropriate severe-hypertension protocol while supporting airway and circulation. Involve senior obstetric, anaesthetic and neonatal teams, monitor fetal recovery and plan delivery after maternal stabilisation.
Phenytoin is not first-line prophylaxis for eclampsia, and obtaining imaging must not delay treatment of severe hypertension. Brain imaging can follow if red flags suggest another neurological cause.
Delivery is necessary, but an uncontrolled airway, seizure risk and BP are immediate hazards. Stabilise the mother before deciding the safest timing and route of birth.
Blood-pressure control alone cannot prevent recurrent eclamptic seizures. Magnesium sulfate is indicated after a first eclamptic event rather than after waiting for another seizure.
Benzodiazepines may be needed for prolonged or ongoing convulsions, but magnesium sulfate is preferred for eclampsia-specific treatment. Ongoing pregnancy without senior review is unsafe.
pearl: Eclampsia treatment prioritises maternal resuscitation, magnesium sulfate and BP control before planned delivery.
pivot: Investigate other causes of seizure if atypical features emerge, without delaying initial eclampsia treatment.

steps: Call
Activate the emergency obstetric response, protect the airway and position the patient safely.
Treat seizures
Start protocol-based magnesium sulfate, monitor breathing, reflexes, urine output and signs of toxicity.
Control pressure
Treat persistent severe hypertension with an appropriate obstetric agent while avoiding sudden hypotension.
Deliver
After stabilisation, assess the fetus and make a timely birth plan with senior obstetric and anaesthetic staff.
management.safety: Adjust magnesium maintenance in renal impairment and monitor for toxicity; fetal bradycardia may improve after maternal resuscitation.
management.local: Follow the linked Australian guidance and current local specialist protocols.

skill: Acute angle closure / time-critical sight preservation
stem: A 69-year-old develops severe left eye pain, blurred vision with rainbow haloes and vomiting after a cinema visit. The eye is red with a cloudy cornea, shallow anterior chamber and mid-dilated poorly reactive pupil. Measured intraocular pressure is 54 mmHg on the left and 17 mmHg on the right.
ask: Which treatment pathway is MOST appropriate?
options: Start cycloplegic and steroid drops for presumed uveitis, with pressure review after inflammation improves.
Use pilocarpine drops alone now, reserving systemic agents until the very high pressure begins to fall.
Begin urgent pressure-lowering treatment and obtain immediate ophthalmology input for definitive angle-opening care.
Schedule routine visual-field testing, because a high-pressure episode commonly settles without lasting optic injury.
Start topical antibiotics for possible keratitis and postpone pressure-lowering treatment until cultures are available.
explanations: An anterior uveitis pathway does not treat the pupil-block and markedly elevated pressure described. Cycloplegia may worsen some acute angle-closure mechanisms, making it unsafe without specialist assessment.

Pilocarpine may be ineffective when the intraocular pressure is extremely high due to iris sphincter ischaemia. It should not be used as sole emergency therapy; specialist-directed pressure reduction is required.

Correct: urgent ophthalmology assessment and immediate aqueous suppressants, with systemic acetazolamide when appropriate, aim to lower the pressure and protect vision. Once feasible, laser peripheral iridotomy or another specialist-selected intervention treats the underlying closure.
Delay risks irreversible optic nerve damage. Visual fields are important in chronic glaucoma follow-up but have no priority over pressure-lowering treatment of this acute painful red eye.
Eye infection may cause pain and corneal haze, but the shallow chamber, mid-dilated pupil and severe IOP elevation identify an acute angle-closure emergency. Antibiotics alone will not lower IOP.
pearl: Acute angle closure presents with a painful red eye, haloes, nausea, mid-dilated pupil and markedly elevated IOP.
pivot: If a secondary mechanism such as topiramate-related uveal effusion is suspected, pilocarpine and definitive procedures may differ.

steps: Identify
Assess visual acuity, pupils and IOP if safe; avoid pharmacological pupil dilation and contact ophthalmology urgently.
Lower pressure
Begin local protocolled aqueous-suppressing drops and systemic acetazolamide if appropriate and not contraindicated.
Reassess
Treat nausea and pain, monitor IOP and visual acuity and escalate if pressure remains high.
Definitive care
Arrange peripheral iridotomy or the appropriate specialist procedure and assess fellow-eye risk.
management.safety: Pilocarpine may be ineffective at high IOP and inappropriate in secondary angle closure. Avoid delaying urgent specialist referral.
management.local: Follow the linked Australian guidance and current local specialist protocols.
